content: Steroid-sparing strategies have been explored in recent years to reduce the adverse effects associated with long-term steroid use in kidney transplant recipients. However, previous systematic reviews have demonstrated a significant increase in the risk of acute rejection when steroids are withdrawn after kidney transplantation. Various protocols exist for steroid withdrawal, and their potential benefits and risks require systematic evaluation. This review is an update of a prior analysis first published in 2009. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and harms of steroid withdrawal or avoidance in kidney transplant recipients. A comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register up to February 15, 2016, using relevant search terms. Randomised and quasi-randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving steroid avoidance or withdrawal at any time after kidney transplantation were included in the analysis. Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias and extracted data, resolving any disagreements through discussion. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model. Dichotomous outcomes were reported as relative risk (RR), and continuous outcomes were expressed as mean difference (MD), both with 95% confidence intervals. The review included 48 studies (224 reports) involving 7,803 randomised participants, of which three studies (346 participants) were conducted in children. The 2009 review had included 30 studies (94 reports, 5,949 participants). Among the included studies, 19 had a low risk of bias for sequence generation, and 14 had a low risk for allocation concealment. Incomplete outcome data were adequately addressed in 22 studies, and 37 studies were free of selective reporting. The studies evaluated three comparisons: steroid avoidance versus steroid maintenance, steroid withdrawal versus steroid maintenance, and steroid avoidance versus steroid withdrawal. In adult studies, there was no significant difference in patient mortality between steroid withdrawal and steroid maintenance (10 studies, 1,913 participants; death at one year post-transplantation: RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.30) or between steroid avoidance and steroid maintenance (10 studies, 1,462 participants; death at one year post-transplantation: RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.80). Similarly, no significant difference in graft loss was observed between steroid withdrawal and steroid maintenance (8 studies, 1,817 participants; graft loss excluding death with functioning graft at one year post-transplantation: RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.92) or between steroid avoidance and steroid maintenance (7 studies, 1,211 participants; graft loss excluding death with functioning graft at one year post-transplantation: RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.86). However, the risk of acute rejection was significantly higher in patients treated with steroids for less than 14 days after transplantation (7 studies, 835 participants; RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.30) and in those who underwent steroid withdrawal at a later time point after transplantation (10 studies, 1,913 participants; RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.61). There was no evidence to suggest a difference in adverse events, such as infections or malignancies, in adult kidney transplant recipients. The effects of steroid withdrawal in pediatric patients remain unclear. In conclusion, this updated review provides further evidence that steroid avoidance and withdrawal after kidney transplantation significantly increase the risk of acute rejection. There was no evidence of a difference in patient mortality or graft loss up to five years post-transplantation. However, the long-term consequences of steroid avoidance and withdrawal remain uncertain due to the lack of prospective long-term studies.
